title: Alexandre Santos — Frontend Engineer and Architect
content: I build fast, accessible, maintainable web interfaces. Before code, I spent 18 years designing buildings. Both disciplines taught me the same lesson: good structure stays invisible, yet you feel it in every interaction.

title: Introduction
content:
I am a Senior Frontend Engineer with more than 9 years of experience building high-traffic web platforms, and a registered architect (Ordem dos Arquitectos n.º 20022). I live in Vila Nova de Gaia, Porto.

For 7 years at 7Graus, I was the primary owner of client-side performance across more than 50 portals serving over 29 million monthly active users. I looked after loading speed, visual stability, and interaction responsiveness (Core Web Vitals), supported daily releases, and designed a multi-brand design system shared across teams.

Outside employment, I run ibid., an independent software studio where I build my own products end to end: from product concept and UI design through automated testing, continuous delivery, and web or app-store releases. This site presents that software work first.

Before software, I worked as an architect and project manager: coordinating architects, engineers, and contractors, municipal licensing, and technical specifications within budgets and schedules. That career forms the second half of the site.

I work primarily with TypeScript, Angular, Web Components (Lit), React, SCSS, Three.js/WebGL, Node.js, NestJS, Vitest, Playwright, GitHub Actions, and Firebase.

GitHub · LinkedIn · Download CV (PDF) · Get in touch via the contact form in the closing section.

title: Oh Save Me! — local-first personal finance
content:
A personal and family finance assistant that answers questions like “can I afford a holiday this month?” instead of handing you a spreadsheet.

Oh Save Me! imports bank statements and categorizes transactions directly on the user's device. Data never leaves the device for analysis: it lives in a local database (RxDB on IndexedDB) and syncs solely through the user's own Google Drive, in a private vault and optionally in a shared vault with another person.

The app learns from user corrections: bank column detection and category suggestions run locally. The codebase follows domain, application, infrastructure, and UI layers, backed by 18 automated Playwright journeys including an accessibility audit.

A single codebase targets four platforms: web (Firebase Hosting), Android and iOS (Capacitor 8), and macOS (Tauri 2). The web build and Android and macOS installers are produced automatically on every release.

What it demonstrates: local-first offline architecture, domain-driven design, conflict-resolving sync, cross-platform delivery, end-to-end testing, and accessibility.

Technologies: Angular 22 (signals, standalone), strict TypeScript, RxDB, IndexedDB, Capacitor, Tauri, Google Drive API, Vitest, Playwright, ibid-ui design system.

Live demo · Code on GitHub

title: Papikapi — papercraft app, studio and API
content:
A children's habit app where the reward is a real-world object: a paper figure the child cuts out and builds together with their parents.

Papikapi (app)

A parent types a short note — “tidied up the toys and hugged their brother” — and the app suggests which behaviors were practiced and how many points they earn; the parent simply confirms. Points unlock figures that rotate in 3D on screen and export to a printable sheet. No account or backend server is required: data stays on the phone and syncs between both parents through a file in their Google Drive. The child only sees their own view; the parent area sits behind its own tab. Angular 22, RxDB, three.js, Capacitor, and Tauri.

Papikapi Studio

The web studio where figures are created and verified: model catalog, prompt-based generation, live step-by-step progress, and interactive 3D and animated assembly preview with three.js.

Papikapi API

A NestJS API and five-stage pipeline that takes a text description or reference images and produces the illustration, 3D mesh, simplified textured model, 2D unfold, printable A4 PDF booklet, and animated assembly plan. Heavy compute stages run on-demand GPU workers (RunPod Serverless) billed per second, logging cost and duration for every figure. SQLite with Drizzle, Server-Sent Events progress streaming, Docker, and a Bruno collection covering every endpoint.

What it demonstrates: end-to-end product thinking (from privacy guarantees to unit economics), 3D on the web, a multi-language processing pipeline (TypeScript, Python, Blender), and cloud GPU cost control.

Live demo · App on GitHub · Studio on GitHub · API on GitHub

title: ibid-ui Design System and Boilerplate
content:
The component library giving every ibid. product a shared visual language and consistent behavior.

ibid-ui is an Angular design system structured into atoms, molecules, and organisms: buttons, form inputs, data tables, bar and line charts, bottom sheets, navigation, voice dictation, and more. Styles follow ITCSS architecture and BEM naming, built on color, typography, and spacing tokens with runtime theme switching. Every component carries unit tests and a Storybook entry.

Boilerplate serves as both the starting template for every new product and the live showcase of the design system: an Angular application pre-wired with routing, navigation, i18n, theme switching, and a dedicated route per component family. Its Storybook acts as the public catalog of the design system.

What it demonstrates: reusable component architecture, scalable CSS, runtime theming, accessibility, and living documentation — translating the multi-brand design system work at 7Graus into a visible, inspectable system.

Public Storybook · Public Boilerplate

title: ibid-workspace — monorepo, architecture and CI/CD
content:
The shared workspace where all products live together, share code, and are tested and released automatically.

ibid-workspace is a modular monorepo where each app and library is its own repository mounted as a git submodule. Strict dependency rules keep boundaries intact: an app can import from any library, a library never imports from an app, and cross-project imports always go through workspace aliases. Shared libraries provide the design system, core services (i18n, theming, translation, voice, Google Drive sync), test engines (axe-core accessibility audits and device-specific journey recording), and dependency-free utilities.

Continuous integration in GitHub Actions runs only the checks affected by each change, enforcing lint limits, Vitest unit tests, and Playwright journeys across mobile, tablet, and desktop. Versioning is automated from commit messages; each release deploys web builds to Firebase Hosting, builds Android APKs and macOS installers, publishes Storybook, and mirrors projects to their standalone repositories. Scheduled dependency updates and CI jobs execute on a self-hosted Docker runner.

What it demonstrates: code organization at scale, enforced module boundaries, cross-product sharing, and automated testing and delivery.

Technologies: strict TypeScript 6, Angular 22, Vitest, Playwright, Storybook 10, ESLint, commitlint, Husky, GitHub Actions, Docker, Firebase Hosting, Capacitor, Tauri.

title: Architecture and Project Management Career
content:
From 1999 to 2017 I worked in architecture: design, municipal permitting, technical specification, and construction supervision. That background shapes how I structure software today.

Multidisciplinary coordination. Managed architectural projects and municipal licensing alongside architects, engineers, and contractors within strict budgets and deadlines.

Technical specification. Specified building systems and bills of quantities on large-scale developments, aligning technical standards across multiple specialist teams.

Technical and commercial consulting (Grupo Sosoares, 2011–2012). Advised architects and contractors on aluminum and glass facade systems: detailing, thermal and daylight performance, cost estimates, and site follow-up.

qb arquitectura + design (2007–2011). Collaborating architect and co-author across residential housing, refurbishment, social facilities, illustration, and 3D visualization.

WS and P4 — corporate office interiors for international organizations. At these two studios I worked on the design and refurbishment of workplaces for telecommunications operators, an investment bank headquarters, an oil and gas company, and a global consultancy. The layouts balanced institutional identity with flexible work areas and dense technical infrastructure.

Roots. The family construction business Veríssimo & Filho, with more than 50 years in operation, gave me an early grounding in construction detail and site craft.

Bridge into software. While practicing architecture, I began building parametric layouts and 3D presentation tools for permitting, sparking the transition into software engineering.

Architectural toolset: AutoCAD, Revit, 3ds Max, Artlantis, Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign. Registered member of Ordem dos Arquitectos n.º 20022.

title: Cacilhas riverfront — urban plan and music center
content:
Academic master's project in Architecture (Universidade Lusíada, 2008): an urban plan for the northern riverfront of Almada between Cacilhas and Porto Brandão, paired with a contemporary music center beside the Cacilhas ferry terminal.

Almada's northern riverfront sits cut off from the rest of the city by the cliff face and the Tagus river, preserving steam-era industrial ruins. The proposal takes that heritage of innovation as its starting point: rather than erasing what stands there, it adds a new layer for contemporary life connected to information networks.

The urban plan (“Terminal”) reconnects both banks and settlements along the cliff through pedestrian routes, public plazas, and a landmark lighthouse. Built above the new intermodal ferry terminal, the contemporary music center combines concert halls, an outdoor auditorium, a media library, and dance studios with framed views toward the river.

What it shows an employer: framing a complex problem with many stakeholders, defining a phased delivery strategy, and carrying design from masterplan down to construction detail.

title: Housing Balance Manifesto
content:
Portugal is losing large numbers of young people. Many leave because they cannot afford a home. This manifesto explains the crisis with official figures and outlines proposals to solve it. Sourced numbers are cited in brackets like [1]. All proposals are the author's own and labeled as Proposal.

1. The country is losing its young people

Every year around 65,000 to 70,000 people leave Portugal. In 2024 the figure was roughly 65,000, down 5,000 from 2023 [1][2]. At the height of the financial crisis in 2013, more than 120,000 emigrated [3].

Today around 1.8 million people born in Portugal live abroad [4].

Those leaving are predominantly young. In 2022, 54% of permanent emigrants were aged 20 to 34 [5]. Roughly 30% of people born in Portugal aged 15 to 39 currently live in another country [6].

This carries a steep economic cost. A 2024 study estimated that 194,000 young university graduates emigrated between 2012 and 2021; if they returned, Portugal's economy could grow by an additional 0.65 percentage points per year [7].

The author argues that housing is now the main barrier preventing young people from staying or returning.

2. Paying rent has become impossible

In Lisbon, an average household spends 80% of its income just to pay rent; in Porto, 69% [8]. The recommended threshold is no more than one third of income.

For a young person living alone on a single salary, the rent burden is heavier still.

Buying has grown far harder too. In Q2 2026, the median sale price of dwellings in Portugal reached €2,445 per square meter, up 18.4% year-on-year [9]. In Lisbon city it stands at €5,299/m², topping €6,000/m² across central parishes, while central Porto sits near €4,160/m² [9].

3. Construction costs are not the whole story

Building has become more expensive, driven mainly by labor. New-housing construction costs rose 4% in 2025, and in September 2026 stood 7.4% higher than a year earlier [10][11].

Yet home prices are rising far faster than construction costs: 18.4% versus 7.4% in a single year [9][10].

The author contends that most of this gap comes from land prices and speculation rather than the cost of laying brick on brick.

4. Households are taking on record debt

Portuguese households owe banks €116.8 billion in housing loans as of June 2026, the sharpest annual increase since 2003 [12]. Banks issue more than €2 billion in new mortgages every month [13].

The public state guarantee for young buyers helped many enter the market, but introduced risk: in 2025, 21% of new mortgages went to borrowers at high risk of default, up from roughly 3% in prior years [14][15].

In response, from August 2026 Banco de Portugal capped a household's total debt-service-to-income ratio at 45%, down from 50% [16].

5. A nation of homeowners

In Portugal, 71% of residents live in owner-occupied homes and only 29% rent [17]. Market-rate rentals represent just 16% of housing [17].

Other European countries show a different balance: in Germany, 53% of people rent; in Austria, 46% [17][18].

With so few rental homes available, people starting out have little alternative to buying.

6. Tourism adds pressure

Tourism matters deeply to the economy. In 2025, tourist accommodation logged 89.7 million overnight stays, up 1.6% from 2024 [19]. Accommodation revenues rose from roughly €6.7 billion in 2024 to €7.2 billion in 2025 [20][21].

Many homes that could house residents have shifted to visitor stays, especially in city centers. Informal, unregistered rentals also remain outside official figures.

7. The proposals

This section sets out the author's proposals. All figures, targets, and timelines below are author estimates and design choices rather than official statistics.

Proposal 1 — A Housing Stabilization Fund

Proposal: establish a self-funding vehicle with zero public debt, financed by idle properties and urban plots, tourism activity, and land-value capture.

The fund operates in two phases. Phase 1 covers Years 1 to 3. Phase 2 begins in Year 5 and runs permanently. By Phase 2, a major share of revenue comes from the fund itself: rents on its homes and repayments of its loans.

Revenue source (€ million per year)Phase 1 (Years 1–3)Phase 2 (Year 5 onward)
Levy on idle urban plots (~40,000 plots)75050
Vacant homes and regularization of informal leases (~250,000 units)650150
VAT adjustment on tourist accommodation from 6% to 13%420450
€5/night levy in pressured municipalities (~76M nights), plus €500/year on select residence permits*430450
35% land-value capture on PDM reclassifications, plus 4% IMT surcharge on homes above €1M1,300650
Loan repayments from SMEs and builder consortia—450
Rents from 100,000 fund-owned homes (€420/month average)—504
75-year ground-lease rights on auctioned land—250
Guarantee fund yield—150
Total3,5503,154

* Residence permits granted via investment, digital-nomad visas, or preferential tax regimes.

The idle-land levy is assessed on permitted buildable capacity across an estimated €15 billion base: 5% in Year 1, 10% in Year 2 if unused, rising up to 15%.

Loans to SMEs and builder consortia total €600 million per year at 2% interest over 30-month cycles. Plots left idle for 24 months move to public auction.

Target: deliver 52,000 homes per year under the 80/20 model until 35% of the stock is regulated rental housing, reducing new annual bank mortgage lending by €8–10 billion.

Proposal 2 — The 80/20 model

Proposal: in every new development:

80% of homes are affordable rentals, capped at 25% of household income.

20% of homes remain on the open market.

Portugal previously tried another path: INH and PER social housing estates concentrated low-income households in single-use districts far from services and jobs. The 80/20 model prevents segregation by mixing households of diverse incomes within the same building.

Proposal 3 — Property tax that compensates rather than punishes

Current law permits municipal property-tax (IMI) surcharges of up to 920% on vacant homes and urban plots in high-pressure areas. In December 2025, Portugal's tax arbitration court (CAAD, Case 640/2025-T) ruled that surcharge disproportionate and unconstitutional [22][23]. The ruling applies to that case, though the issue may reach the Constitutional Court [24].

Proposal: shift the logic of the charge.

Compensation, not punishment. An idle urban plot in a pressured zone leaves already-paid public infrastructure unused: water, sewage, power, and roads. The fee compensates that waste.

Progressive and fair. Rates of 5%, 10%, and 15%, assessed on real buildable capacity.

Ends immediately. The levy stops the day the owner files a valid prior notice and breaks ground within 24 hours, or contributes the plot to the fund's Partnership Pool—paying zero upfront and receiving 20% to 25% of completed dwellings.

Fast appeal. CAAD arbitration in 90 days, with collection suspended against a standard bank guarantee—ending “pay first, appeal later.”

Revenues stay local. Proceeds go directly into ring-fenced municipal accounts where collected.

Proposal 4 — Detecting informal rentals

Proposal: water and electricity utilities report aggregate household usage per dwelling (via CPE and CUI meter codes).

1. If a property shows sustained family-level utility consumption while no one holds tax residency or a registered lease there, the owner receives an electronic notice.

2. The owner has 30 days to reply—explaining, for example, a work relocation or a loan to an immediate relative (verified automatically)—or register the lease.

3. Without response, the vacant-property surcharge applies as a rebuttable presumption.

Tenants can also initiate regularization: via open banking, showing recurring monthly payments to the landlord's IBAN plus a utility contract in their name enables the Tax Authority to issue the lease, securing at least 5 years of stability and access to Porta 65 support.

Every step must respect data protection. Portugal's data authority (CNPD) already reviewed similar measures under “Mais Habitação” (Opinion 50/2023) [25]. European open banking rules follow PSD2, and upcoming EU payment regulations give users a central consent dashboard [28][29].

Proposal 5 — Modular construction and merit-based licensing

Proposal: factory-built homes. Modular systems built from ISO shipping containers or light-gauge steel frames cut construction time from 24–36 months to 6–8 months and lower costs by up to 25%.

Seismic safety: ductile steel and bolted module connections comply with Eurocode 8.

Energy: 70–100 mm exterior PIR insulation achieves low heat loss (U below 0.25 W/m²K) and NZEB energy performance.

Acoustics: floating floors and double boards with mineral wool.

Today, Law 41/2015 governs builder eligibility and IMPIC issues contractor licenses [26].

Proposal: merit-based contractor licensing. Consortia led by architects or engineers registered with their professional Orders may qualify without prior corporate turnover or equity. Designs are submitted in open BIM/IFC and verified automatically within 15 working days. Innovative methods are reviewed by technical panels appointed by the professional Orders alongside LNEC, IST, and FEUP, while the fund finances university-born construction startups.

Proposal 6 — 24-hour permitting with mandatory 10-year insurance

Permitting currently takes 12 to 36 months—a delay the author estimates adds 15% to 20% to final home prices.

Proposal: 24-hour prior notice. Where an approved masterplan exists (PDM, subdivision, or detailed plan), filing a compliant notice takes legal effect in 24 hours, with the professional Order certifying compliance within 48 hours.

Mandatory 10-year insurance. For serious structural defects, the insurer repairs or pays out within 60 days and recovers later if a designer acted with gross negligence.

Strict accountability. False declarations trigger a disciplinary ruling by the Order within 30 days and license suspension for 2 to 10 years.

Municipalities on 80/20 too. 80% of municipal technical staff focus on proactive planning—detailed plans, subdivisions on municipal land, and infrastructure—while 20% conduct on-site inspections and random audits.

3D zoning rules. Each plot's envelope is published as open 3D GIS/BIM rules showing exact buildable volume.

France has operated a similar framework since 1978 under the Spinetta Law, requiring builders to hold dommages-ouvrage insurance so ten-year defect repairs are paid immediately without waiting for fault litigation [27].

Proposal 7 — Social support

Proposal: an annual €1.4 billion support package reaching more than 350,000 people.

8. The software tool — Solum

To put this model into practice, the author is building dedicated software: Solum.

Proposal: Solum helps manage the 80/20 housing model, calculate income-indexed affordable rents, and track construction progress and social supports—designed throughout around strict data protection.

9. Conclusion

Portugal educates skilled young people and then watches them leave. Housing is one of the primary reasons.

Official data shows housing prices outpacing both wages and construction costs, rising household debt, and an acute shortage of rental homes.

This manifesto sets out a practical path: more homes at rents people can actually pay, simpler rules to build, fair taxation of idle capacity, and targeted support for those who want to stay or return.

title: The ibid. Practice
content:
ibid. comes from the Latin ibidem, meaning “in the same place.” It is the thread connecting my work in architecture and software: building atop what already exists, with respect for the people who inhabit it.

We live across two spaces: the physical place our bodies occupy and the digital networks carrying our work, conversations, and livelihoods. Architecture is not merely a container for life; it can mediate between those two spaces. Software can too.

From that idea come four practical rules:

1. Never start from a blank slate. Every city, like every codebase, is built in layers. Before proposing anything, I read what is already there—the terrain, the history, the code, the people—and add a new layer that allows it to keep evolving.

2. Place matters. In a world of uniform global flows, value lies in what is specific: the culture of a site, the real needs of a family, the working context of a team. That is why my products keep user data on the user's own device.

3. Bridge the disciplines. Splitting knowledge into silos that no longer speak to each other is a paradox of the knowledge society. Good work brings specialists, decision-makers, and end users together in a shared language everyone understands.

4. A dialogue between maker and user. A work only communicates when it connects the author's intent with the user's experience inside its real environment. I design interfaces the same way: made to be read, used, and corrected by the people who rely on them.

ibid. is where I put these ideas to the test in real products with automated testing and delivery—and it is how I want to contribute inside a product engineering team.
